newsitem.title: USA: Simplify school lunch operations, U.S. group says.
newsitem.headline: Simplify school lunch operations, U.S. group says.

text.p: Local operators of the school lunch program suggested Tuesday a major simplification in rules -- giving meals to poor children for free and charging full price to their more affluent classmates.
At present, the 94,000 schools in the program must employ a three-tier system of free, reduced price and full-price meals.

Leaders of the American School Food Service Association raised the idea of a two-tier price plan during a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing. They suggested a number of other steps to simplify the program as well.

Agriculture chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, said the hearing "gives us ample time" to compile ideas for a reauthorization due in 1998 of several public-feeding programs. The Agriculture Department spends more than $38 billion a year on school lunch, food stamps and other nutrition assistance.
"We would like to explore with the committee whether it is possible to reduce our three-tier system...to a two-tier system," said ASFSA president Janet Bantley.

Many children of the "working poor" cannot afford the 40-cent charge for reduced price meals, Bantly said, which reduces their access to food. In addition, she said child-nutrition programs were time-consuming to administer. Schools must determine eligibility every day for pupils.

More than 26 million children eat hot meals each day through the school lunch program. Half of the meals are free to poor children. To qualify for free meals, a family of four must have an income of $20,280 or less. For reduced price meals, their income must be $28,850 or less.
